Series::hardsigmoid¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series Series::hardsigmoid() const
Series& Series::hardsigmoid_() const

A Clipped Linear Gate¶

hardsigmoid() applies a piecewise-linear approximation to a smooth sigmoid:

hardsigmoid(x) = 0             when x <= -3
                 x / 6 + 1/2  when -3 < x < 3
                 1             when x >= 3

It is intended for gates and bounded activations where the strict [0, 1] range matters but an exponential is unnecessary. Values at or below -3 are closed off, values at or above 3 are fully open, and the six-unit middle interval changes at constant slope. Use sigmoid() when a smooth curve and non-zero tails matter more than the cheaper linear middle branch.

The operation is elementwise, out of place, and shape preserving. Real floating input retains its dtype. Integral and Boolean input promote to float32; this is essential because interior values such as 1 map to 2/3, not to an integer. Complex input is invalid because the branch tests require an ordered real value. Empty and higher-rank inputs follow the same elementwise contract without special flattening or reduction.

The result is newly allocated on the receiver’s platform. Saturated values are exactly zero or one in the output dtype; they are not merely close to those bounds.

Reverse Mode And Boundaries¶

The local derivative is

1 / 6    when -3 < x < 3
0        otherwise

Both endpoints belong to the saturated branches, so the recorded derivative at exactly -3 and exactly 3 is zero. The second derivative is zero wherever the first derivative is classically defined; the two corners remain non-differentiable branch boundaries.

In-Place Form¶

hardsigmoid_() is the in-place sibling of hardsigmoid(): it computes the same result and writes it back into self directly — mutating it (and any other handle sharing the same storage) instead of allocating a new Series — then returns a reference to self.

Despite being declared const at the call site — a quirk of how this method’s wrapper is generated, not a promise that self is left unchanged — hardsigmoid_() genuinely mutates the series it’s called on.

auto x = pluss::make_series({-4.0, 0.0, 4.0});
x.hardsigmoid_();
std::cout << x;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 0.5, 1]

Examples¶

Example 1. This vector includes both saturated regions, both exact boundaries, and three interior points.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({-4.0, -3.0, -1.5, 0.0, 1.5, 3.0, 4.0})
        .hardsigmoid());

Output¶

Series(shape=[7], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=7, contiguous=true)
data=[0.0000, 0.0000, 0.2500, 0.5000, 0.7500, 1.0000, 1.0000]

Example 2. Integer matrices preserve shape and promote to float32 so the interior fraction survives.

auto y = pluss::make_series({{-6, -3, 0}, {1, 3, 6}}).hardsigmoid();
pluss::series::print(std::cout, y);
std::cout << "dtype=" << y.scalar_type() << " dim=" << y.dim()
          << " shape=[" << y.size(0) << ',' << y.size(1) << ']';

Output¶

Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float32, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=
⎡ 0.0000 0.0000 0.5000 ⎤
⎣ 0.6667 1.0000 1.0000 ⎦
dtype=float32 dim=2 shape=[2,3]

Example 3. Reverse mode makes the open-interval boundary rule explicit.

auto x = pluss::make_series({-4.0, -3.0, -1.0, 0.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);
x.hardsigmoid().sum().reverse();
pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.sensitivity());

Output¶

Series(shape=[7], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=7, contiguous=true)
data=[0.0000, 0.0000, 0.1667, 0.1667, 0.1667, 0.0000, 0.0000]

Example 4. Chaining the result as a gate keeps the bounded factor in the Series graph.

auto logits = pluss::make_series({-6.0, 0.0, 6.0});
auto payload = pluss::make_series({10.0, 20.0, 30.0});
pluss::series::print(std::cout, payload.mul(logits.hardsigmoid()));

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0.0000, 10.0000, 30.0000]

See Also¶

  • sigmoid() provides the smooth logistic curve.

  • hardswish() multiplies the input by this gate.

  • clamp_min() and clamp_max() provide the two one-sided bounds used to build a clamp without applying the middle rescaling.
